content.title: Logging & Monitoring: Reading the Evidence

prequestion.prompt: Before reading: a server records 2,000 failed logins in one night. What does that tell you on its own?
options: The server has definitely been breached
Not enough yet — you need to know where they came from, which accounts, and whether any succeeded
Nothing — failed logins are harmless because they failed

content.reading_markdown:
## Logs are the record of what happened

Every system can write down what it does: who signed in, what was changed, which connections were made. Those **logs** are how you detect an attack in progress and how you reconstruct one afterwards. A system that does not log, or whose logs nobody reads, can be breached without anyone ever knowing.

## What is worth logging

- **Authentication** — sign-ins that succeed and fail, and where they came from.
- **Privilege changes** — accounts created, added to admin groups, or given new rights.
- **Configuration changes** — firewall rules, security settings, software installed.
- **Access to sensitive data**, and the security tools' own alerts.

## From scattered logs to a SIEM

A single server's log shows one corner of the picture. A **SIEM** (security information and event management) system **collects** logs from across the organisation, **normalises** them into one format, **correlates** events from different sources, and **raises alerts** when a pattern matches a rule. Correlation is the valuable part: a failed VPN login, then a success from the same address, then a new admin account on a file server, means little in three separate logs and a great deal side by side.

Two things make correlation possible. **Synchronised clocks** — every system set from the same time source, or events cannot be put in order. And **protected logs** — sent to a separate store as they are written, so an intruder who gains admin rights cannot quietly delete the evidence. Logs are kept for a defined **retention** period, long enough to investigate an incident found months later.

Too many low-value alerts cause **alert fatigue**: analysts start ignoring them. Tuning rules so alerts are rare and meaningful is part of the job.

## Reading for a brute-force attack

MITRE ATT&CK catalogues password attacks under **Brute Force (T1110)**. Two patterns are worth knowing by shape:

- **Password guessing** (T1110.001) — many attempts against one or a few accounts, usually from the same source, in a short time.
- **Password spraying** (T1110.003) — one or two common passwords tried against many accounts, slowly, to stay under lockout limits.

When you investigate, answer four questions from the log itself: **where** the attempts came from, **how many** there were, **which accounts** were tried, and **over what time span**. Then ask the question that matters most: did any attempt from that source **succeed**?

## Worked example

A web portal's log shows 40 failed sign-ins for the account "finance" between 02:14:05 and 02:14:45, all from 198.51.100.23, then a successful sign-in for "finance" from the same address at 02:15:10. One account, one source, forty attempts in forty seconds: password guessing. The success afterwards turns a noisy attack into a confirmed compromise — the account is disabled, the session is killed, and the incident response playbook starts.

gate.prompt: An alert says someone may be guessing SSH passwords on this server. Investigate /var/log/auth.log in the terminal, then record your findings below. Only your findings are scored — the commands you type are not.
hints: Before you count anything, filter the log down to the lines that describe the suspicious activity, so you are not mixing it with normal sign-ins.
Treat the last question separately from the counts: look for any line from that same source that records a different kind of event from the ones you counted.

slot_labels: Source IP address of the failed attempts
Seconds from the first to the last failed attempt
Did any attempt from that address succeed? (yes / no)

gate.accessible_equivalent: The auth.log is also available as a plain-text listing readable by a screen reader, with the same five labelled answer fields; scored identically as correct_slot_ratio. Commands are never required.

analog_synthesis.prompt: Away from the screen, write out by hand eight lines of an invented sign-in log for a small office: some normal sign-ins and one password-spraying attempt (one password tried against many accounts). Then hand it to yourself the next morning, or to a friend, and answer the four investigation questions — where from, how many, which accounts, over what time — plus whether anything succeeded.
analog_synthesis.calibration_question: Before checking: could you tell the spraying lines from the normal ones by looking at one line, or only by looking at several lines together — and what does that say about why a SIEM correlates events?
analog_synthesis.accessible_equivalent: Dictate the invented log and the answers to the five questions, or read them aloud with a partner who checks each answer against the lines.

drills.prompt: Complete: A SIEM collects logs, normalises them, ______ events across sources and raises alerts. So many low-value alerts that analysts stop reading them is alert ______. Systems must share a time source, or events cannot be put in ______.
drills.accessible_equivalent: The same blanks as labelled text fields with screen-reader labels; scored identically as correct_slot_ratio.
drills.explanation: Correlation is what a SIEM adds over reading logs one by one; alert fatigue is why rules need tuning; without synchronised clocks a timeline is guesswork.

drills.prompt: Sort each pattern seen in sign-in logs under the attack it most likely shows.

Password guessing: 60 failed sign-ins for 'admin' in two minutes from one address
Repeated failures for one user's account, every few seconds, from one source
Password spraying: One failed sign-in each for 300 different accounts, spread over an afternoon
Two attempts per account across the whole staff directory, spaced to avoid lockouts
Normal activity: A user fails once, then succeeds a minute later from their usual laptop
Staff signing in from the office between 08:00 and 09:00

drills.accessible_equivalent: Keyboard-navigable list pairing each item with one of {Password guessing, Password spraying, Normal activity}; scored identically as bucket_assignment.
drills.explanation: Guessing hammers few accounts quickly; spraying touches many accounts lightly to dodge lockout; a single mistyped password followed by success from a known device is ordinary.

drills.prompt: Without notes: say what events are worth logging, what a SIEM does with them, why clocks and log protection matter, and the questions you would answer from a log to investigate a suspected brute-force attack.
drills.accessible_equivalent: Spoken response transcribed via speech-to-text and scored on the same keyword set.
drills.explanation: Knowing what to log, why correlation needs synchronised, protected logs, and the where / how many / which accounts / when / did-it-succeed questions is the core of first-line monitoring.
